description: Nitrogène is a passionate team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We aim to use NASA Earth observation data and innovative technologies to develop sustainable agricultural solutions. Driven by science, creativity, and teamwork, we welcome motivated members interested in coding, data analysis, design, environmental science, and agriculture. Together, we transform space data into real-world impact and contribute to a more resilient and sustainable future.
summary: Morocco has long been facing water scarcity, while severe floods have also damaged agricultural land and crops. As Moroccan society and economy depend heavily on agriculture production, these challenges threaten the country’s economy and people’s quality of life. Having grown up in the Gharb region, where agriculture is deeply rooted in our identity, we wanted to use technology to contribute to the future of our region. This inspired us to develop Nitrogen, a free, multilingual web tool that helps farmers make informed crop-planning decisions using NASA earth observation data. Farmers select their zone, soil type, last three crops, sowing season and available irrigation water. The tool ranks the 3 best crops for that field and explains the irrigation method, crop rotation rules and the reasons behind each recommendation. It shows local rain, heat, evaporation, soil moisture and vegetation greenness. Our goal is to help farmers make better decisions, protect their land and water, and strengthen our region's agricultural resilience against future climate-related challenges
details:
We developed the Nitrogen website to help farmers in the Gharb region choose the most suitable crops for their fields. Farmers enter five types of information: their location (Kenitra, Sidi Slimane, Sidi Kacem, Souk El Arbaa, Mechra Bel Ksiri or Sidi Yahya El Gharb), soil type (Tirs, Hamri, Dehs, Rmel or Merja), the last two or three crops planted, the sowing season and the available irrigation water. Based on these inputs, the tool recommends the three most suitable crops and explains why they were selected. It also provides irrigation recommendations, crop rotation guidelines, a water balance comparing crop requirements with expected rainfall and available irrigation water, and a list of crops that should be avoided during that season. To make these recommendations, each crop receives a score out of 100, based on four criteria: soil suitability (30%), crop rotation (30%), water availability (30%) and market considerations (10%). We also included rotation rules such as avoiding repeated crops from the same family, respecting minimum breaks between crops.

To support our recommendations with reliable environmental information, we made use of freely available NASA Earth observation data:

NASA POWER: We used rainfall, maximum and minimum temperatures, and root-zone soil wetness data from 2015 to 2024. We also estimated reference evapotranspiration (ET0) using the FAO-56 Hargreaves-Samani method.

SMAP: We used satellite soil moisture data at 9 km resolution to provide an indication of soil moisture conditions.

MODIS: We used vegetation greenness (NDVI) data at 250 m resolution to show vegetation conditions across the different zones.

GPM: We used satellite precipitation estimates to analyze rainfall amounts and patterns across the zones.

SMAP and MODIS data were extracted using NASA AppEEARS. We calculated seasonal averages for six locations and stored the results in our database.

To develop our decision support tool, we used Python and FastAPI for the backend and scoring system, HTML and JavaScript for the interface, and GitHub Pages for hosting. We also used Google Maps satellite imagery to identify our geographical reference points.

Through Nitrogen, we wanted to make satellite information useful and understandable for farmers, especially small and medium-sized farmers who may not have access to advanced agricultural tools. The tool helps them compare different crop options, understand their water requirements and make better use of the resources available to them. In the long term, it's going to contribute to better crop planning, healthier soils and more resilient agriculture in the Gharb region.

What makes our project special is the way we bring together two things that are not always easily connected: farmers' traditional knowledge and NASA Earth observation data. Instead of simply displaying satellite information, we transform it into practical recommendations that farmers can actually use. We also wanted the tool to be accessible to our local community, so we made it simple, free and available in Arabic, French and English, without requiring farmers to have any technical knowledge.

Throughout the development of Nitrogen, we took into consideration the different soil types and farming conditions across the Gharb, as well as seasonal changes, rainfall, temperature, water availability, previous crops and market needs. We also wanted to help farmers better prepare for future challenges, such as droughts and floods, by making more informed crop choices and reducing potential losses.
